title: Genesis 11 — Babel and the line to Abram

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֥י כָל־הָאָ֖רֶץ שָׂפָ֣ה אֶחָ֑ת וּדְבָרִ֖ים אֲחָדִֽים׃

i18n.en: The whole land was of one lip and one set of words.

paragraphs.commentary: **The opening claim is doubled.** *Safa achat* — *one lip* — and *devarim achadim* — *one set of words*. The two phrases name distinct dimensions of linguistic unity. *Safa* — שָׂפָה — is literally the speech-organ ('lip'); the metonymy for *language* is well-attested in Hebrew (cf. Isa 19:18 'the lip of Canaan' = the Canaanite language). *Devarim* — דְּבָרִים — is *words / matters / things*. The doubled claim is: the whole land had not only a shared phonology and grammar (one *lip*) but a shared semantic stock (one set of *words / matters*). // The verse stands in tension with 10:5, 10:20, 10:31, which described the Japhethites, Hamites, and Shemites as already differentiated by *tongues* (*lashon*). The chapter is opening a parallel timeline — or the redactor has preserved two distinct traditions about linguistic origins, with the Table of Nations chapter and the Babel chapter belonging to different source-strands. The standard scholarly attribution: chapter 10 is the Priestly (P) ethnography; chapter 11:1–9 is the Yahwist (J) etiology. The redactor placed them side-by-side and left the seam visible.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְהִ֖י בְּנָסְעָ֣ם מִקֶּ֑דֶם וַֽיִּמְצְא֥וּ בִקְעָ֛ה בְּאֶ֥רֶץ שִׁנְעָ֖ר וַיֵּ֥שְׁבוּ שָֽׁם׃

i18n.en: As they journeyed from the east, they found a valley in the land of Shinar, and they settled there.

paragraphs.commentary: **Eastward, or from the east?** מִקֶּדֶם *miqedem* has the same ambiguity here as in 2:8 (where the garden was planted *miqedem*): it can mean *from the east* (the people are coming westward from a more easterly origin) or *eastward* (they are journeying in an eastward direction). The standard reading is *from the east* — the post-Flood humans, descending from Noah's ark on the mountains of Ararat (8:4) in the Armenian highlands, are migrating south and west into the Mesopotamian alluvium. // *Biqah b'eretz Shinar* — *a valley in the land of Shinar*. The same Shinar named in 10:10 (the location of Nimrod's Babel, Erech, Akkad, Calneh). The chapter is geographically continuous with chapter 10's Nimrod parenthesis: the same southern-Mesopotamian alluvial plain, the same proto-civilization context. *Biqah* — *valley, plain* — names the flat alluvium itself; the contrast with Levantine hill-country is implicit.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ אִ֣ישׁ אֶל־רֵעֵ֗הוּ הָ֚בָה נִלְבְּנָ֣ה לְבֵנִ֔ים וְנִשְׂרְפָ֖ה לִשְׂרֵפָ֑ה וַתְּהִ֨י לָהֶ֤ם הַלְּבֵנָה֙ לְאָ֔בֶן וְהַ֣חֵמָ֔ר הָיָ֥ה לָהֶ֖ם לַחֹֽמֶר׃

i18n.en: They said each to his neighbor, "Come, let us make bricks, and burn them in fire." The brick was for them as stone, and the bitumen was for them as mortar.

paragraphs.commentary: **The first human cohortative.** *Havah nilbenah* — *come, let us make bricks*. *Havah* (an interjection, 'come!') plus the first-person plural cohortative *nilbenah*. The verb is built on the same noun *l'venah* (brick); the wordplay is *nilbenah l'venim* — *let us brick bricks*. The doubled construction repeats in the next clause: *nisrefah lisrefah* — *let us burn (them) with a burning*. // The chapter is opening on a HUMAN cohortative — *let us...* — that will be echoed structurally three times: here (v3), in the city-and-tower decision (v4 *havah nivneh*), and then mirrored from the divine side (v7 *havah neredah*). The cohortative becomes the chapter's rhetorical signature, and the chapter ends by showing the divine cohortative answering the human ones. // *Ha-l'venah l'aven v'ha-chemar laya lahem la-chomer* — *the brick was for them as stone, and the bitumen as mortar*. The aside is technological-archaeological: it notes that the southern Mesopotamian builders, lacking stone (the alluvium has none), substituted kiln-fired clay brick with bitumen mortar. This is empirically accurate to the construction methods of southern Mesopotamian ziggurats, attested archaeologically and in Mesopotamian texts. The chapter is technically literate about the construction methods of the world it describes.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּאמְר֞וּ הָ֣בָה ׀ נִבְנֶה־לָּ֣נוּ עִ֗יר וּמִגְדָּל֙ וְרֹאשׁ֣וֹ בַשָּׁמַ֔יִם וְנַֽעֲשֶׂה־לָּ֖נוּ שֵׁ֑ם פֶּן־נָפ֖וּץ עַל־פְּנֵ֥י כָל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: They said, "Come, let us build for ourselves a city, and a tower with its top in the skies; and let us make for ourselves a name, lest we be scattered upon the face of the whole land."

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's keystone verse — three intentions stated in one breath.** // First, *havah nivneh lanu ir umigdal* — *come, let us build for ourselves a city and a tower*. The pair *ir* (city) and *migdal* (tower) names the political-architectural project. *Migdal* is the ziggurat — the stepped temple-platform of Mesopotamian religious architecture, exemplified by the great ziggurat of Etemenanki at Babylon (the Esagila complex), the most famous of which was rebuilt by Nebuchadnezzar II in the 6th c. BCE. The chapter is reading the ziggurat-tradition, not inventing it. // Second, *v'rosho bashamayim* — *with its top in the skies*. *Rosho* (its head/top) reaching *bashamayim* (in the skies). The phrase is not necessarily a literal claim that the tower will physically reach the heavens; *rosho bashamayim* is a stock-phrase for *very tall* (cf. Deut 1:28, 9:1, of fortified cities 'whose walls reach up to the skies'). But in this chapter the phrase carries more than hyperbole: the ziggurat's *function* was to be a stairway between earth and the divine realm — the Mesopotamian theology of the ziggurat is that the deity descended onto the platform-shrine at its summit, and that human worship ascended through it. *Rosho bashamayim* is naming the ziggurat's *aspiration*, not just its dimension. // Third, *v'na'aseh lanu shem* — *and let us make for ourselves a name*. This is the chapter's most lens-charged phrase. The cohortative *naase* — *let us make* — is the same form as Genesis 1:26's *naase adam* — *let us make humankind*. There it was the Elohim speaking; here it is humans. The chapter is staging humans assuming the divine cohortative register — the *naase adam* of creation is mirrored by the *naase lanu shem* of the post-Flood project. The verbal parallel is exact, and the chapter is silent about whether to read this as imitation, presumption, or aspiration. // *Shem* — *name* — in Hebrew Bible idiom is not just an identifying label but renown, reputation, lasting memory (cf. 2 Sam 7:9, of YHWH making David's *shem* great). The phrase *anshei ha-shem* — *men of name* — was applied in 6:4 to the antediluvian *gibborim*; now in 11:4 the post-Flood humans propose to *make for themselves a name*. The chapter is connecting the human ambition at Babel to the *gibborim*-class register the Flood was supposed to have ended. // *Pen-naputz al-pnei kol ha-aretz* — *lest we be scattered upon the face of the whole land*. The motive is given as fear of dispersion. The verb *putz* (to scatter, disperse) will return in v8 (*vayyafetz YHWH otam*) — what they feared is what happens, brought about by the very God they were trying to overshoot.

paragraphs.text: וַיֵּ֣רֶד יְהוָ֔ה לִרְאֹ֥ת אֶת־הָעִ֖יר וְאֶת־הַמִּגְדָּ֑ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר בָּנ֖וּ בְּנֵ֥י הָאָדָֽם׃

i18n.en: YHWH came down to see the city and the tower which the sons of the human had built.

paragraphs.commentary: ***Vayered YHWH*** — *YHWH came down*. The verb is יָרַד *yarad* — *descend* — used here with YHWH as subject. The anthropomorphic register is plain: YHWH is positioned *above*, the city-and-tower is *below*, and YHWH *descends* to see it. The descent is the inverse of the tower's ascent: the humans build *upward* (with its top in the skies); YHWH comes *down* to inspect. The verbal pairing is the chapter's structural irony — the tower designed to reach the divine realm prompts the divine being to descend, with results the humans did not intend. // The descent-language will recur in v7 (*havah neredah* — *let us go down*) when YHWH speaks in the divine cohortative. The chapter has two descents: v5 (singular YHWH *yarad* — sees) and v7 (plural *neredah* — acts). // *Bnei ha-adam* — *the sons of the human / sons of humankind*. The phrase emphasizes the lineage: these are descendants of the *adam* of Genesis 2–3. The chapter is connecting Babel-builders to the Edenic origin — they are doing what humans do, building what humans build, asserting what humans assert.

paragraphs.text: וַיֹּ֣אמֶר יְהוָ֗ה הֵ֣ן עַ֤ם אֶחָד֙ וְשָׂפָ֤ה אַחַת֙ לְכֻלָּ֔ם וְזֶ֖ה הַחִלָּ֣ם לַעֲשׂ֑וֹת וְעַתָּה֙ לֹֽא־יִבָּצֵ֣ר מֵהֶ֔ם כֹּ֛ל אֲשֶׁ֥ר יָזְמ֖וּ לַֽעֲשֽׂוֹת׃

i18n.en: YHWH said, "Behold — one people and one tongue for all of them! And this is what they begin to do — and now, nothing will be withheld from them which they have schemed to do."

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's load-bearing claim.** YHWH's assessment has three components. // First, *am echad v'safa achat l'kulam* — *one people and one tongue for all of them*. The unity is named twice — *one people, one tongue*. The verse is acknowledging that unified human coordination is what enables what follows. // Second, *zeh hachilam la'asot* — *this is what they begin to do*. The verb הֵחֵל *hechel* — *began* — is the same verb that opened the Nimrod parenthesis (*hu hechel lihyot gibbor*, 10:8). The chapter is reading the Babel project as the *beginning* of unified human technological-political ambition, not the end of it. // Third, the keystone clause: *v'atah lo yibatzer mehem kol asher yazmu la'asot* — *and now, nothing will be withheld from them which they have schemed to do*. The verb בָּצַר *batsar* — *to restrain, hold back, make inaccessible* — appears in the passive niphal (*yibatzer*): nothing will *be made inaccessible* to them. The clause is YHWH's plain claim that human coordination at this scale produces unlimited capacity. The verb *yazmu* (from *zamam*, 'devise, scheme, plan') is neutral-to-negative in its semantic range — it covers planning generally but is often used of *premeditation* in legal contexts. // The Wheel of Heaven reading hears this verse with unusual clarity. The divine assessment is *not* that what the humans are doing is metaphysically wrong (no curse-language is used, no judicial register); it is that what they are doing is *technologically open-ended*. The response in v7 will be a deliberate intervention to break the coordination — not a punishment but a *cap on capacity*. The chapter is staging a strategic divine response to human power-aggregation. The lens reads this against the canon's framing of the Elohim as a senior civilization that has reasons to manage human technological progress.

paragraphs.text: הָ֚בָה נֵֽרְדָ֔ה וְנָבְלָ֥ה שָׁ֖ם שְׂפָתָ֑ם אֲשֶׁר֙ לֹ֣א יִשְׁמְע֔וּ אִ֖ישׁ שְׂפַ֥ת רֵעֵֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: "Come, let us go down and confuse their tongue there, so that they may not understand each other's tongue."

paragraphs.commentary: **The third explicit divine cohortative in Genesis.** *Havah neredah v'navlah* — *come, let us go down, and let us confuse*. // The first was 1:26 — *naase adam b'tsalmenu kidmutenu* (*let us make humankind in our image, in our likeness*) — at the creation of humankind. The second was 3:22 — *hen ha-adam haya k'achad mimennu lada'at tov vara* (*behold, the human has become like one of us, knowing good and bad*) — after the Tree-eating. The third is 11:7. All three are first-person *plural* speech with divine subject. // The pattern across the three: at 1:26 the divine plural *makes* humankind; at 3:22 the divine plural recognizes that humankind has become *like* the divine plural in a specific capacity; at 11:7 the divine plural intervenes to *cap* what humankind can do together. The Genesis primaeval-history arc, on the chapter's textual surface, is the story of a divine-plural class managing the emergence of a human-collective whose capacity is approaching theirs. The chapter does not editorialize on this reading; it preserves the grammatical plural and lets the reader draw the structural pattern. // The cohortative *havah neredah* — *come, let us go down* — is the mirror of the humans' *havah nilbenah* (v3) and *havah nivneh* (v4). The chapter has stacked four cohortatives in nine verses: two human (let us brick / let us build), two divine (let us go down / let us confuse). The verbal symmetry is the chapter's most precise structural feature. The humans' cohortative-projects produce a divine cohortative-response. The chapter is composed with a careful sense of rhetorical match. // *V'navlah sham sefatam* — *let us confuse their tongue there*. The verb בָּלַל *balal* — *mix, confound, confuse* — is the etymological root of *Babel* (v9). The intervention is *linguistic*: not destroying the city, not killing the builders, but breaking the *coordination capability* by fragmenting the shared language. The response is targeted: it removes the specific affordance that made the project possible.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֨פֶץ יְהוָ֥ה אֹתָ֛ם מִשָּׁ֖ם עַל־פְּנֵ֣י כָל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וַֽיַּחְדְּל֖וּ לִבְנֹ֥ת הָעִֽיר׃

i18n.en: YHWH scattered them from there upon the face of the whole land, and they ceased to build the city.

paragraphs.commentary: **Their fear is fulfilled by the divine action.** The humans had said in v4: *pen-naputz al-pnei kol ha-aretz* — *lest we be scattered upon the face of the whole land*. The verse now reports: *vayyafetz YHWH otam ... al-pnei kol ha-aretz* — *YHWH scattered them ... upon the face of the whole land*. The exact phrase the humans had used in their fear-clause is now used in the action-clause, with YHWH as the subject of the verb the humans had used in the passive. // The verb is the same root (פוץ *putz*); the humans feared the dispersal that the divine action then produced. The chapter is reading the Babel project as motivated by the fear of dispersion, and the divine response as enacting exactly what the project was designed to prevent. // *Vayyachdelu livnot ha-ir* — *and they ceased to build the city*. The verb *chadal* (cease) is the gentlest possible language for project-stop: not destroyed, not punished, not killed. The construction simply *halts* when the linguistic coordination fails. The chapter is technically accurate about the social mechanism: large-scale construction projects collapse when communication breaks down. The divine intervention is engineering-grade: minimal, targeted, sufficient.

paragraphs.text: עַל־כֵּ֞ן קָרָ֤א שְׁמָהּ֙ בָּבֶ֔ל כִּי־שָׁ֛ם בָּלַ֥ל יְהוָ֖ה שְׂפַ֣ת כָּל־הָאָ֑רֶץ וּמִשָּׁם֙ הֱפִיצָ֣ם יְהוָ֔ה עַל־פְּנֵ֖י כָּל־הָאָֽרֶץ׃

i18n.en: Therefore its name was called Babel, because there YHWH confounded the tongue of the whole land; and from there YHWH scattered them upon the face of the whole land.

paragraphs.commentary: **The etymology and the closing summary.** *Babel* — בָּבֶל — and *balal* — בָּלַל — share a triconsonantal root structure (b-b-l / b-l-l) close enough for the chapter to assert an etymological pun. The actual etymology is contested: the Hebrew *Babel* most likely derives from the Akkadian *Bab-ilim* (*'gate of the gods'*) — the same name that gives English *Babylon*. The chapter is offering a *folk etymology* that recodes the city's name from *gate of the gods* (the Mesopotamian self-naming) into *the place of confusion* (the Hebrew Bible's reframing). The pun is theological re-naming: the Mesopotamian city of divine access is recast as the city of divine refusal of access. // The chapter closes the Babel narrative and pivots to the Shem-genealogy that will land at Abraham. The reader is to keep two things in view: (1) the divine assessment that human coordination at scale was approaching divine capacity, and (2) the divine response of fragmentation. The line that will run from v10 down to v26 — Shem to Abram — is the *new* divine project after the cap was imposed. The chapter's structural logic: humanity *en masse* could not be permitted to continue at Babel; the next chapter will start the *covenant-line* of Abraham. The two are sequential narrative moves.

paragraphs.text: אֵ֚לֶּה תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת שֵׁ֔ם שֵׁ֚ם בֶּן־מְאַ֣ת שָׁנָ֔ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־אַרְפַּכְשָׁ֑ד שְׁנָתַ֖יִם אַחַ֥ר הַמַּבּֽוּל׃

i18n.en: These are the begettings of Shem. Shem was one hundred years old when he fathered Arpachshad, two years after the deluge.

paragraphs.commentary: **The toledot of Shem opens.** This is the fifth *toledot* in Genesis (after 2:4 of the skies, 5:1 of Adam, 6:9 of Noah, 10:1 of Noah's sons). The genealogy that follows is the structural counterpart to chapter 5: ten generations, each with the formula *X lived Y years, fathered Z; and X lived W years after fathering Z, and fathered sons and daughters*. The pattern is identical to chapter 5; what differs is the *length* of lives — the post-Flood lifespans drop steadily across the ten generations from ~600 (Shem) down to ~205 (Terah, v32). // *Shenatayim achar ha-mabbul* — *two years after the deluge*. The dating-by-Flood-event continues the chronological grid of chapter 5–9; it also closes the chronological loop: the Flood is the anchor-event, with all subsequent dates measured from it.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִי־שֵׁ֗ם אַֽחֲרֵי֙ הוֹלִיד֣וֹ אֶת־אַרְפַּכְשָׁ֔ד חֲמֵ֥שׁ מֵא֖וֹת שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Shem lived after he fathered Arpachshad five hundred years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.text: וְאַרְפַּכְשַׁ֣ד חַ֔י חָמֵ֥שׁ וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־שָֽׁלַח׃

i18n.en: Arpachshad lived thirty-five years and fathered Shelach.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִ֣י אַרְפַּכְשַׁ֗ד אַֽחֲרֵי֙ הוֹלִיד֣וֹ אֶת־שֶׁ֔לַח שָׁלֹ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֔ים וְאַרְבַּ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Arpachshad lived after he fathered Shelach four hundred and three years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.text: וְשֶׁ֥לַח חַ֖י שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־עֵֽבֶר׃

i18n.en: Shelach lived thirty years and fathered Eber.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִי־שֶׁ֗לַח אַחֲרֵי֙ הוֹלִיד֣וֹ אֶת־עֵ֔בֶר שָׁלֹ֣שׁ שָׁנִ֔ים וְאַרְבַּ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Shelach lived after he fathered Eber four hundred and three years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִי־עֵ֕בֶר אַרְבַּ֥ע וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־פָּֽלֶג׃

i18n.en: Eber lived thirty-four years and fathered Peleg.

paragraphs.commentary: **Eber, the eponymous Hebrew ancestor.** עֵבֶר *Eber* is the etymological source most commonly proposed for עִבְרִי *Ivri* (Hebrew), the gentilic that Abraham will be called in 14:13. The chapter places Eber in the central position of the Shem-genealogy: four generations after Shem, with Abraham coming four generations after Eber. The genealogy is structured to make Eber the symbolic midpoint between the post-Flood patriarch and the covenant-founder.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִי־עֵ֗בֶר אַחֲרֵי֙ הוֹלִיד֣וֹ אֶת־פֶּ֔לֶג שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֔ה וְאַרְבַּ֥ע מֵא֖וֹת שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Eber lived after he fathered Peleg four hundred and thirty years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִי־פֶ֖לֶג שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־רְעֽוּ׃

i18n.en: Peleg lived thirty years and fathered Reu.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִי־פֶ֗לֶג אַחֲרֵי֙ הוֹלִיד֣וֹ אֶת־רְע֔וּ תֵּ֥שַׁע שָׁנִ֖ים וּמָאתַ֣יִם שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Peleg lived after he fathered Reu two hundred and nine years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.commentary: **The lifespans drop.** Peleg's total lifespan (239 years) is less than half of his great-grandfather Shem's (600 years). The compression of post-Flood lives — already attested in chapter 5 with Adam's 930 and Methuselah's 969 — is accelerating in chapter 11. By Terah (v32, 205 years), the antediluvian-scale lifespans are gone. The chapter does not comment on the compression. The patriarchal narratives that follow (Abraham 175, Isaac 180, Jacob 147) will continue the decline.

paragraphs.text: וַיְחִ֣י רְע֔וּ שְׁתַּ֥יִם וּשְׁלֹשִׁ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־שְׂרֽוּג׃

i18n.en: Reu lived thirty-two years and fathered Serug.

paragraphs.text: וַיְחִ֣י רְע֗וּ אַחֲרֵי֙ הוֹלִיד֣וֹ אֶת־שְׂר֔וּג שֶׁ֥בַע שָׁנִ֖ים וּמָאתַ֣יִם שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Reu lived after he fathered Serug two hundred and seven years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.text: וַיְחִ֥י שְׂר֖וּג שְׁלֹשִׁ֣ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־נָחֽוֹר׃

i18n.en: Serug lived thirty years and fathered Nachor.

paragraphs.text: וַיְחִ֣י שְׂר֗וּג אַחֲרֵ֛י הוֹלִיד֥וֹ אֶת־נָח֖וֹר מָאתַ֣יִם שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Serug lived after he fathered Nachor two hundred years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.text: וַיְחִ֣י נָח֔וֹר תֵּ֥שַׁע וְעֶשְׂרִ֖ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֖וֹלֶד אֶת־תָּֽרַח׃

i18n.en: Nachor lived twenty-nine years and fathered Terah.

paragraphs.text: וַיְחִ֣י נָח֗וֹר אַחֲרֵי֙ הוֹלִיד֣וֹ אֶת־תֶּ֔רַח תְּשַֽׁע־עֶשְׂרֵ֥ה שָׁנָ֖ה וּמְאַ֣ת שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֥וֹלֶד בָּנִ֖ים וּבָנֽוֹת׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Nachor lived after he fathered Terah one hundred and nineteen years, and fathered sons and daughters.

paragraphs.text: וַֽיְחִי־תֶ֖רַח שִׁבְעִ֣ים שָׁנָ֑ה וַיּ֙וֹלֶד֙ אֶת־אַבְרָ֔ם אֶת־נָח֖וֹר וְאֶת־הָרָֽן׃

i18n.en: Terah lived seventy years and fathered Abram, Nachor, and Haran.

paragraphs.commentary: **The decade-genealogy lands at the threshold.** The ten-generation sequence from Shem to Abram parallels the ten-generation sequence from Adam to Noah in chapter 5. The structural parallel is deliberate: each ten-generation arc anchors a turning point — Noah for the Flood, Abram for the covenant. // *Abram* enters Genesis here, the first explicit mention. The reader who has been following the toledot-arc since chapter 5 has been waiting for this moment for two chapters. The naming triad — Abram, Nachor, Haran — places Abram first by prominence (not necessarily by birth-order; *vayyoled et X et Y v'et Z* is the standard naming-by-importance pattern, as with Shem-Ham-Yepheth).

paragraphs.text: וְאֵ֙לֶּה֙ תּוֹלְדֹ֣ת תֶּ֔רַח תֶּ֚רַח הוֹלִ֣יד אֶת־אַבְרָ֔ם אֶת־נָח֖וֹר וְאֶת־הָרָ֑ן וְהָרָ֖ן הוֹלִ֥יד אֶת־לֽוֹט׃

i18n.en: These are the begettings of Terah. Terah fathered Abram, Nachor, and Haran; and Haran fathered Lot.

paragraphs.commentary: **The sixth toledot in Genesis opens.** The chapter has now stacked three toledot-formulae in two chapters (10:1 Noah's sons; 11:10 Shem; 11:27 Terah), each narrowing the focus: from the post-Flood world to the Shemite line to the household of Terah. The narrowing prepares the move from cosmic-ethnographic scope to family-narrative scope that will run through chapters 12–50.

paragraphs.text: וַיָּ֣מָת הָרָ֔ן עַל־פְּנֵ֖י תֶּ֣רַח אָבִ֑יו בְּאֶ֥רֶץ מוֹלַדְתּ֖וֹ בְּא֥וּר כַּשְׂדִּֽים׃

i18n.en: Haran died in the presence of Terah his father, in the land of his birth, in Ur of the Kasdim.

paragraphs.commentary: **The first recorded child-predeceasing-parent in Genesis.** *Vayyamat Haran al-pnei Terah aviv* — *Haran died in the presence of Terah his father*. The phrase *al-pnei* (literally 'upon the face of') in the context of death means *during the lifetime of* — Haran predeceased his father, the reverse of the patriarchal-norm in which the father dies first. The narrative aside marks the death as out-of-order. // *Ur Kasdim* — *Ur of the Kasdim*. Ur was the great Sumerian city of southern Mesopotamia, capital of the Third Dynasty of Ur (ca. 2100 BCE), excavated by Leonard Woolley in the 1920s. The qualifier *Kasdim* (Chaldeans) is anachronistic: the Chaldeans are a first-millennium-BCE Aramean people who came to dominate Babylonia in the Neo-Babylonian period. *Ur Kasdim* is therefore a chronologically-confused identifier — the city of Ur but with its later-conquering people's name attached. Modern scholarly debate has proposed alternative identifications (a northern Mesopotamian *Ur* near Haran, rather than the famous southern *Ur*) precisely to avoid the *Kasdim* anachronism. The chapter is naming the family's place of origin in Mesopotamia, with vocabulary that mixes geographic eras. The Wheel of Heaven lens reads Abram's family as Mesopotamian in origin — the same alluvial plain that hosted Nimrod's Babel — preparing the reader for chapter 12's move out of that civilization.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח אַבְרָ֧ם וְנָח֛וֹר לָהֶ֖ם נָשִׁ֑ים שֵׁ֤ם אֵֽשֶׁת־אַבְרָם֙ שָׂרָ֔י וְשֵׁ֤ם אֵֽשֶׁת־נָחוֹר֙ מִלְכָּ֔ה בַּת־הָרָ֥ן אֲבִֽי־מִלְכָּ֖ה וַֽאֲבִ֥י יִסְכָּֽה׃

i18n.en: Abram and Nachor took for themselves wives. The name of Abram's wife was Sarai, and the name of Nachor's wife was Milkah, daughter of Haran, the father of Milkah and the father of Yiskah.

paragraphs.commentary: **The brides are named — and one is identified.** Sarai's lineage is not given; Milkah's is (she is Haran's daughter, niece to her husband Nachor — an intra-family marriage consistent with patriarchal-period norms). *Yiskah* is named only here in the Hebrew Bible; rabbinic tradition identifies her with Sarai (no textual evidence), or as a separate sister. The brevity is one of the chapter's textual cruces — the chapter leaves the relationship unresolved. // The naming of the wives anticipates Genesis 12+: Sarai will be central to the Abraham narrative; Milkah will be referenced again only as Rebekah's grandmother (24:15). The chapter is setting up the patriarchal family network through which the covenant will be transmitted.

paragraphs.text: וַתְּהִ֥י שָׂרַ֖י עֲקָרָ֑ה אֵ֥ין לָ֖הּ וָלָֽד׃

i18n.en: Sarai was barren — she had no child.

paragraphs.commentary: **The chapter's quiet pivot.** Six words in Hebrew set up the entire Abraham-Sarah cycle that will run through chapters 12–25. *Aqarah* — *barren* — names the condition that will be the load-bearing constraint of the next ten chapters: the covenant-line passes through a couple unable to produce children. The whole drama of the Abraham narrative — the divine promise of offspring, the years of waiting, the Hagar and Ishmael episode, the laughter of Sarah, the late birth of Isaac — turns on this single verse. // The redundant *ein lah valad* — *she had no child* — drives the point home: barrenness is the asserted fact, not just delayed conception. The chapter is foregrounding the obstacle the next narrative will overcome.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּקַּ֨ח תֶּ֜רַח אֶת־אַבְרָ֣ם בְּנ֗וֹ וְאֶת־ל֤וֹט בֶּן־הָרָן֙ בֶּן־בְּנ֔וֹ וְאֵת֙ שָׂרַ֣י כַּלָּת֔וֹ אֵ֖שֶׁת אַבְרָ֣ם בְּנ֑וֹ וַיֵּצְא֨וּ אִתָּ֜ם מֵא֣וּר כַּשְׂדִּ֗ים לָלֶ֙כֶת֙ אַ֣רְצָה כְּנַ֔עַן וַיָּבֹ֥אוּ עַד־חָרָ֖ן וַיֵּ֥שְׁבוּ שָֽׁם׃

i18n.en: Terah took Abram his son, Lot the son of Haran his grandson, and Sarai his daughter-in-law, the wife of his son Abram; and they went out with them from Ur of the Kasdim to go to the land of Canaan, and they came to Haran and settled there.

paragraphs.commentary: **The unfinished journey.** Terah, not Abram, is the verse's grammatical subject — *vayyiqach Terah* (Terah took). The family's exit from Ur is at Terah's initiative; Abram is the *passenger* of his father's migration. The destination is *artzah Kena'an* — *toward the land of Canaan* — the same Canaan whose boundaries chapter 10:19 sketched in anticipation. // But they do not arrive. *Vayavo'u ad-Charan vayyeshvu sham* — *they came as far as Haran and settled there*. Haran (חָרָן) is a major northern Mesopotamian city (the site near modern Harran in southeastern Turkey), an important Bronze and Iron Age trading center on the Aramaean / Mesopotamian frontier. The family stops short of Canaan; Terah will die in Haran (v32). The migration toward Canaan is interrupted. // Chapter 12 will open with YHWH's call to Abram to *go from your land, from your kindred, from your father's house, to the land that I will show you* (12:1) — and Abram will *complete* the migration his father had begun and abandoned. The Wheel of Heaven lens reads the seam: the journey toward Canaan begins under Terah's initiative without divine prompting, stalls at Haran, and resumes under explicit divine call. The covenant-line is positioned as completing what the family-line could not.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּהְי֣וּ יְמֵי־תֶ֔רַח חָמֵ֥שׁ שָׁנִ֖ים וּמָאתַ֣יִם שָׁנָ֑ה וַיָּ֥מָת תֶּ֖רַח בְּחָרָֽן׃ (ס)

i18n.en: The days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and Terah died in Haran.

paragraphs.commentary: **The primaeval-history arc closes.** Terah's 205-year lifespan is the chapter's closing data-point; his death in Haran is the chapter's closing event. The primaeval-history block of Genesis 1–11 ends here — at a death, in a transitional city, with a stalled migration. The next chapter opens with the divine call that will turn the family's incomplete journey into the foundational journey of the patriarchal narrative. // The transition from primaeval history to patriarchal narrative is structurally clean: Genesis 1–11 has moved from cosmos (ch 1) to humanity (chs 2–3) to family (chs 4–5) to the cosmic reset (chs 6–9) to the ethnographic catalogue (ch 10) to the Babel cap (ch 11:1–9) to the genealogy (11:10–26) to the household-narrative threshold (11:27–32). Each successive section narrows the scope. Chapter 12 will narrow further: from Terah's whole household to a single called man — Abram — and a single destination — the land YHWH will show him.
